how-much-to-charge-for-a-dog-walk.html.text:
← Dog walking route pricing calculator

How much to charge for a dog walk

Every answer to this question online is a range: fifteen to thirty dollars for a half-hour walk, more in cities. The range is not wrong, and it is not usable, because it hides the variable that actually decides whether your day pays — and that variable is not the walk.

Open the free route pricing calculator

A 30-minute walk is 40 minutes of your time

The walk is what the client books. The job is the walk plus getting there. At a 10-minute drive, a 30-minute visit commits 40 minutes, so a quarter of the time you are being paid for is spent in the car — before mileage, which is a separate cost on top.

LineAmount
Committed time (30 min walk + 10 min drive)40 minutes
Labor (0.67 hr × $24/hr target)$16.00
Mileage (4 miles × $0.67)$2.68
Overhead share ($45/month over 60 visits)$0.75
Cost to deliver$19.43
Margin (15%)$2.91
Price$22.34
Effective hourly rate on the walk itself$33.52

That last row is the one worth sitting with. The visit earns $33.52 per hour of walking — a good-looking number — and $22.34 for two thirds of an hour of your actual life. Both are true. Only the second one fills a calendar.

The route-density trap

Now change one input and nothing else. Same walk, same dog, same rate, same margin — only the client's distance moves:

Drive each wayCommittedMileageCostPrice
5 minutes (2 miles)35 min$1.34$16.09$18.50
10 minutes (4 miles)40 min$2.68$19.43$22.34
20 minutes (9 miles)50 min$6.03$26.78$30.80

The same 30-minute walk is a $18.50 job and a $30.80 job. One flat rate across a scattered client book means your close clients are quietly subsidising your far ones — and the far ones are why the week feels full while the month does not pay. Route density is worth more than your headline rate, and it is the one lever a marketplace listing cannot pull for you.

Three ways to handle it, in rough order of how well they hold up. A distance-based fee names the cost the client is actually creating and leaves nearby clients on a competitive rate. A service radius declines the work rather than pricing it, which is often right for a one-visit-a-week client forty minutes out. Raising the base rate for everyone to cover the worst commute is the common choice and the weakest one: it overprices the neighbours who book five times a week and refer the rest of the street.

What a target income actually costs in visits

Pricing one visit well is half the question. The other half is how many of them a target income needs. A book of four recurring clients — two at five visits a week, one at three, one at two — is 65 visits a month at an average price of $23.09:

FigureValue
Visits per month65
Average price per visit$23.09
Monthly route revenue$1,501.15
Target monthly income$3,000.00
Gap$1,498.85
Additional visits needed65 per month

Sixty-five more visits a month is fifteen a week — and, not coincidentally, it is the book over again. Doubling a client list is a different kind of plan from "earn another $1,500 a month", and it is the honest shape of that target: roughly three more daily clients, or two more plus a weekend block. That is a concrete thing to go and do. The revenue gap on its own is not, and it is the form the number usually arrives in.

Multi-dog households

A second dog in the same house adds handling effort and nothing else: no extra drive, no extra stop, no extra travel time. Charging a second full visit price for it is the fastest way to lose a household that would otherwise be one of your densest, most reliable clients. A per-additional-pet surcharge on top of the base visit reflects the real extra cost, which is why it is its own input rather than a multiplier.

Common questions

How much should I charge for a 30-minute dog walk?

There is no single answer, because the walk is not the whole job. Price the time you commit, which is the walk plus the drive to reach it, then add mileage, your share of monthly overhead, and a margin. At a 24 dollar an hour target rate, a 30-minute walk with a 10-minute drive and 4 miles of travel costs 19.43 dollars to deliver and prices at 22.34 dollars with a 15 percent margin. The same walk for a client five minutes away prices at 18.50 dollars, and for one twenty minutes away at 30.80 dollars.

Why does the same dog walk cost different amounts for different clients?

Because drive time is part of the job and it is not the same for every client. A 30-minute walk with a 10-minute drive is 40 minutes of committed time, so a quarter of what you are being paid for is spent in the car. Doubling the drive to 20 minutes makes it 50 minutes and adds mileage on top. Charging one flat rate across a scattered client book means the close clients subsidise the far ones, and the far ones are the reason the day feels full and the month does not pay.

Should I charge a travel fee or raise my base rate?

A distance-based fee is usually the fairer and more defensible of the two, because it names the cost the client is actually creating and leaves your close clients paying a competitive rate. Raising the base rate across the book to cover the worst commute overprices everyone near you, which is exactly the segment most likely to book several visits a week and refer neighbours. The alternative to either is a service radius: decline what falls outside it rather than pricing for it.

What is route density and why does it matter more than my rate?

Route density is how much drive time separates consecutive visits. It matters more than your headline rate because it changes how many visits fit in a day and how much of each visit you are paid for driving. Four clients within five minutes of each other can be served in a block where drive time nearly vanishes between them; four clients spread across a city cannot, whatever you charge. Tightening the geography of the book raises earnings without raising a single price, which is the one lever a marketplace listing cannot pull for you.

How many dog walking visits do I need for a target monthly income?

Divide the gap between your current route revenue and your target by your average visit price. A book of four recurring clients doing 65 visits a month at an average of 23.09 dollars brings in 1,501.15 dollars. Reaching 3,000 dollars a month means closing a gap of 1,498.85 dollars, which at that average price is 65 more visits a month, or 15 more visits a week. Seeing the visit count rather than the revenue gap is what makes the target concrete, because visits are what has to fit in a calendar.

Does an extra dog in the same household double the price?

No, and pricing it that way loses bookings. A second dog in the same house adds handling effort but no extra drive, no extra travel time, and no extra stop, so a per-additional-pet surcharge on top of the base visit reflects the real extra cost far better than a second full visit price does. The surcharge is a separate input for exactly that reason: it lets a multi-dog household stay good value to the client and still pay you for the extra work.

Run it on your own route

The calculator prices one visit from your own times, rates and overhead, rolls a recurring client list into monthly revenue, and tells you how many more visits a target income needs. It runs entirely in your browser.

Open the free route pricing calculator

Weighing this against a marketplace listing? See this calculator vs. Rover.

Common questions

Why does drive time count as billable time if I'm not with a dog yet?

Because it is time you cannot spend on another visit or anything else that pays. A route of five stops with ten minutes of driving between each one spends nearly an hour a day just driving — leave that out of the price and every visit is quietly subsidizing the commute to the next one.

Why is an overnight priced with on-call hours instead of just the minutes I'm actually up and working?

An overnight stay commits your whole night to one client even during the hours nothing goes wrong — you cannot book another job, sleep at home, or leave. Pricing only the arrival, walk, and departure minutes treats being on call as free, which is why a flat per-night rate that ignores it usually undercharges the job with the most exposure.

Why does the calculator gross up the price for a payment processing fee instead of just subtracting it from what I planned to charge?

If a payment app takes 3% and you quote the pre-fee number, you net 3% less than you planned on every single visit. Grossing the price up so the fee comes out of the client's payment, not your margin, is the only way the number you typed as your target margin is the number you actually keep.

Does anything about my clients or route get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and the client price/visit rows you type into the route table are never saved anywhere — they exist only in the page while it is open. The visit inputs and the two route settings above the table (weeks per month, target income) are different: those are saved locally on this device, so you don't retype them, and a shareable link can carry them to another device. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-a-flat-per-walk-rate.html.text:
← Dog walking & pet sitting rate calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-walk rate

Names no specific product or company. This compares a free calculator against the generic method every independent walker already has: one flat price — commonly $20 a walk — quoted the same regardless of where the stop is.

First — the flat rate is right, and you should have one

A website, a flyer, or a quick text back to a lead needs a number before you know the address. "$20 a walk" is a perfectly fine headline price, and no calculator replaces having one. What follows is not an argument that the flat rate is wrong. It is what that same number stops showing you the moment a stop is real and you know how far it is from the last one.

The worked example

Both rows below quote the identical $20 walk from this calculator's own starting numbers: 30 on-site minutes, a $24 target hourly rate, $0.67/mile, and $45 of monthly overhead spread across 60 visits. The only thing that changes between them is the drive to reach the stop.

QuestionNearby stop — 10 drive min, 4 mi round tripFarther stop — 25 drive min, 12 mi round trip
What the flat rate charges $20 — the walk $20 — the walk, unchanged
Round-trip mileage cost $2.68 (4 mi × $0.67) $8.04 (12 mi × $0.67) — the flat rate never separates this out
Total minutes the stop occupies 40 min (30 on-site + 10 drive) 55 min (30 on-site + 25 drive)
Overhead allocated to this visit $0.75 ($45 ÷ 60 visits) $0.75 ($45 ÷ 60 visits) — same either way
Break-even cost for this stop $19.43 — just under the $20 flat rate $30.79 — well above the $20 flat rate
What the $20 flat rate actually nets $0.57 above cost — a 2.9% margin, far under a 15% target −$10.79 — a loss on a route stop that looked identical on the price sheet
This calculator's price at a 15% target margin $22.34 $35.41 — $13.07 more than the nearby stop, for the same walk
Effective hourly rate the $20 flat rate actually pays $30.00/hr (40 billed minutes) $21.82/hr — a 27% cut from the nearby stop, at the identical price

The two places the flat rate goes quiet

1. Drive time and mileage never separate from the walk

A flat rate answers "what do I charge for a walk," not "what does it cost me to reach this stop." Both live inside the same $20 either way. The calculator splits them out — $2.68 of mileage on the nearby stop, $8.04 on the farther one — so the drive, the overhead, and the labor are three visible numbers instead of one flat guess that happened to work out.

2. The same price can turn from a thin margin into a loss

This is the one that costs real money over a full route. The flat rate charges $20 whether the stop is five minutes off your last one or twenty-five, but the break-even cost is not the same, so a $20 walk that barely clears cost nearby (by 57 cents) becomes a $10.79 loss once the drive grows — with nothing on the price sheet to say so. A walker filling a day off the flat rate alone can run "the same $20 walk" all afternoon and end the day having lost money on the stops that happened to be spread out.

When the flat rate is still the better tool

For advertising, it plainly is. A website or a flyer cannot show a live calculator, and a new lead calling for a price wants one number, not a form. The sensible arrangement is both: quote the flat rate to get the booking, then run this calculator once you know which stops are on today's route, to check whether that day's version of "the $20 walk" still covers the drive — and, on a stop far enough out, whether it is worth a distance surcharge or a decline instead.

Every figure on this page is this calculator's own worked example, computed from its own default inputs, not a claim about any real walker's business or an industry benchmark. Your rates, mileage, and overhead will produce different numbers — the point is which numbers to produce, not what they should come out to.

Common questions

Is a flat per-walk rate wrong?

No, and it should not go away. A website, a flyer, or a quick text back to a lead needs one number, and "$20 a walk" is a fine headline price. The point of this page is not that the flat rate is wrong — it is that the flat rate is the same number whether the stop is five minutes from your last one or twenty-five, and only one of those two stops actually covers what the visit costs.

How much does drive time actually cost on a route stop?

Two things a flat rate shows neither of: the mileage cost of reaching the stop, and the clock minutes it occupies that could otherwise go to another visit. On this calculator's own defaults, a nearby stop (10 drive minutes, 4 round-trip miles) costs $2.68 in mileage alone on top of 40 total billed minutes. Move the same $20 walk to a stop with 25 drive minutes and 12 round-trip miles and the mileage cost alone triples to $8.04, before the extra 15 minutes of driving is even counted.

Why does the same $20 walk lose money on some stops and not others?

Because the flat price is fixed but the drive behind it is not. At the nearby stop, this calculator's own break-even cost (labor at $24/hr, mileage, and allocated overhead) is $19.43 — so the flat $20 still clears it, by 57 cents, well under the 15% target margin the calculator is priced to. At the farther stop the same $20 walk faces a break-even cost of $30.79 — the flat rate is now $10.79 short of covering the visit at all, a loss on a route that looked identical from the price sheet.

Does the calculator replace the flat rate?

No, and it is not trying to. The flat rate is what you advertise before you know the route. This calculator is what you run once you know which stops are actually on today's route, to check whether that day's version of "the $20 walk" still covers the drive — and, on a stop far enough out, whether it needs a distance surcharge or a decline instead.

vs-rover.html.text:
← Dog walking & pet sitting rate calculator

This calculator vs. Rover

Rover is a marketplace: an app and website where pet owners search for a sitter or walker nearby, message them, book a visit, and pay through Rover's own platform, and where a sitter or walker builds a public profile to be found. It sets the terms of that marketplace itself — its own booking flow, its own payment handling, its own policies for who gets listed. Per Rover's own Help Center, that includes a service fee taken from the sitter or walker's earnings (a standard 20%, dropping to 15% or 10% at higher lifetime booking totals with a client; 25% in California) plus a separate booking fee of up to 11% (capped at $50) charged to the pet owner. This calculator applies none of that — it is for pricing a visit or client relationship directly, on or off any marketplace.

That makes Rover the right tool for finding clients or a sitter in the first place. This calculator answers a different question, for walkers and sitters who already have a client — whether found through Rover, a referral, a flyer, or years of word of mouth: what should this specific visit cost, and does the whole route add up to a living?

QuestionWhere to answer it
Find a new dog-walking or pet-sitting client, or a sitter for my own pet? Rover's marketplace, or another way of finding clients.
Book, message, and collect payment for a visit through a shared app? Rover or a similar booking platform.
How much does Rover's own service fee and booking fee take out of a booking? Rover's published fee schedule — this calculator charges no platform fee of its own.
What should I charge for this specific walk once drive time, extra pets, and overhead are counted? This calculator's per-visit price.
How do I price an overnight stay so being on call all night isn't free? This calculator's on-call-hours field — a flat per-night rate usually skips this.
Does my whole recurring client list add up to my monthly income goal? This calculator's route revenue rollup — a marketplace app prices one booking at a time, not a route.
Price your own visit and route

This tool needs no account, no listing, and no client-matching: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and your client list and prices stay on your device — nothing is uploaded anywhere, and refreshing the page clears the route table on purpose.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Rover?

They answer different questions. Rover is a marketplace: it helps a pet owner find a sitter or walker (or a walker find new clients) and runs the booking, messaging, and payment through its own app and its own fee structure. This calculator has no listings, no booking, and no client-matching at all — it is for a walker or sitter who already has their own clients (found through Rover, referrals, or anywhere else) and wants to price a visit from real time, drive, mileage, extra pets, and overnight on-call hours, then check whether that whole route clears a monthly income goal.

How much does Rover take from a booking?

Per Rover's own Help Center ("What are the service fees?"), the standard service fee taken from a sitter or walker's earnings is 20% (so a provider keeps about 80% of the booking amount), dropping to 15% or 10% at higher lifetime booking totals with a client, plus a separate booking fee of up to 11% (capped at $50) charged to the pet owner on top of the provider's rate. California has its own fee schedule (25%). These figures come from Rover's published policy, change over time and by state, and are not applied anywhere in this calculator — check Rover's current Help Center article for your own situation.

Does this replace Rover, Wag, or a similar app?

No, and it is not trying to. This tool does not list you to new customers, does not process payment, and does not handle insurance, background checks, or booking messages the way a marketplace app does. It only prices a visit and rolls a client list into monthly revenue. Plenty of independent walkers use a marketplace app to find clients and a separate rate calculation to decide what to charge them once found — this is the second half.

Is this page affiliated with Rover?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Rover Group, Inc. Rover is a trademark of Rover Group, Inc., named here only to describe what this calculator is for and is not.
